cards.front: A protein phosphatase removes the phosphate from a protein using {{c1::water}}.
cards.back: Protein-O-PO3(2−) + H2O → protein-OH + Pi
cards.quote: A protein kinase moves the end, or gamma, phosphate of ATP onto the protein; a protein phosphatase removes it with water.
cards.section: Write the mark, erase the mark

cards.front: In animal cells, which residues carry most protein-bound phosphate, and which carries well under 1% of it?
cards.back: Serine and threonine carry most. Tyrosine carries well under 1% (about 2% of mapped sites).
cards.quote: Tyrosine carries well under 1% of it in a cell, about 2% of mapped sites, which kept phosphotyrosine hidden until 1979.
cards.section: Write the mark, erase the mark

cards.front: Why is a phosphate a good regulatory switch on a protein?
cards.back: It adds close to two negative charges near pH 7, ATP is a plentiful donor, and separate enzymes add it (kinase) and remove it (phosphatase).
cards.quote: Near pH 7 the attached phosphate carries close to two negative charges where there were none.
cards.section: Write the mark, erase the mark

cards.front: Why can a cell control adding and removing a protein phosphate independently?
cards.back: Adding transfers phosphate from ATP; removing hydrolyses it with water. They are two different reactions with two different enzymes.
cards.quote: A protein kinase moves the end, or gamma, phosphate of ATP onto the protein; a protein phosphatase removes it with water.
cards.section: Write the mark, erase the mark

cards.front: ATP sits at {{c1::millimolar}} concentration in the cell.
cards.quote: ATP sits at millimolar concentration in the cell.
cards.section: Write the mark, erase the mark

cards.front: Why is the abundance of phosphohistidine in mammalian proteins still unclear?
cards.back: The acid used in standard methods strips the phosphate from histidine.
cards.quote: Mammals also phosphorylate histidine, but the acid in standard methods strips that phosphate, so how common phosphohistidine is remains unclear.
cards.section: Write the mark, erase the mark

cards.front: Does phosphorylation always switch a protein on?
cards.back: No. A phosphate may favor activity or inhibition; it is not an automatic on signal.
cards.why: In muscle, the same mark favors active glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase.
cards.quote: It may favor activity or inhibition; it is not an automatic on signal.

cards.front: Name the four things one added phosphate can do to a protein.
cards.back: Change activity through shape, create a docking site, change location, or prime another modification.
cards.quote: The phosphate has no activity of its own; the protein and its neighbours respond to it.
cards.section: Four consequences of one added phosphate

cards.front: In muscle glycogen phosphorylase, a phosphate on serine 14 is far from the catalytic site. How can it still change activity, and what does the same mark do to glycogen synthase?
cards.back: It acts through shape, favoring the active form of phosphorylase. The same mark inhibits glycogen synthase.
cards.quote: In muscle glycogen phosphorylase the phosphate lands on serine 14, near the chain's start and far from the catalytic site, yet it favors the active form.
cards.section: Four consequences of one added phosphate

cards.front: NFAT is held in the cytoplasm by phosphates that hide its nuclear-entry sequence. If calcineurin is inhibited while the kinases keep working, where does NFAT accumulate?
cards.back: In the cytoplasm. Its phosphates remain, so the nuclear-entry sequence stays hidden.
cards.quote: Its phosphates remain, so the sequence that sends NFAT into the nucleus stays hidden.
cards.section: Four consequences of one added phosphate

cards.front: Glycogen synthase kinase 3 prefers a serine or threonine four residues before a site already phosphorylated by a priming kinase. The priming kinase answers signal A and GSK3 answers signal B. What happens to the substrate if only signal B is present?
cards.back: It is phosphorylated poorly, because GSK3 prefers a primed site and none is present. The substrate can wait for two inputs.
cards.why: Priming means one phosphate prepares a site for another modification.
cards.quote: If the priming kinase answers a different signal, the substrate can wait for two inputs.
cards.section: Four consequences of one added phosphate

cards.front: How can a phosphate create a docking site on a protein?
cards.back: A partner whose pocket recognises the phosphorylated side chain can dock on it.
cards.quote: A partner whose pocket recognises the phosphorylated side chain can dock; a later lesson covers those pockets.
cards.section: Four consequences of one added phosphate

cards.front: In the simplest one-site model with first-order rates, the steady-state phosphorylated fraction is f = {{c1::k(kinase) / (k(kinase) + k(phosphatase))}}.
cards.back: Rate in = k(kinase) × (1 − f); rate out = k(phosphatase) × f; at steady state they match.
cards.quote: f = k(kinase) / (k(kinase) + k(phosphatase))
cards.section: How much protein carries the phosphate?

cards.front: In the one-site first-order model, why does the steady-state phosphorylated fraction depend on the phosphatase as well as the kinase?
cards.back: At steady state rate in equals rate out, so f = k(kinase) / (k(kinase) + k(phosphatase)); the phosphatase rate stays in the denominator.
cards.quote: So the phosphorylation level depends on both the kinase and the phosphatase, not on kinase activity alone.
cards.section: How much protein carries the phosphate?

cards.front: In the one-site first-order model, a kinase works at 0.6 per minute and a phosphatase at 0.2 per minute. A drug cuts only the kinase rate tenfold. Does the phosphorylated fraction fall tenfold?
cards.back: No. f falls from 0.6/(0.6 + 0.2) = 0.75 to 0.06/(0.06 + 0.2), about 0.23: roughly threefold.
cards.why: The phosphatase rate stays in the denominator.
cards.quote: A tenfold cut in kinase rate gives only about a threefold fall, because the phosphatase rate stays in the denominator.
cards.section: How much protein carries the phosphate?

cards.front: In the one-site first-order model, a kinase works at 0.2 per minute and a phosphatase at 0.6 per minute. A drug cuts only the phosphatase rate tenfold. What are the phosphorylated fractions before and after?
cards.back: Before: 0.2/(0.2 + 0.6) = 0.25. After: 0.2/(0.2 + 0.06) = 0.77, about threefold higher. Rests on f = k(kinase)/(k(kinase) + k(phosphatase)).
cards.quote: At steady state the rates match
cards.section: How much protein carries the phosphate?

cards.front: A pathway must shut off within seconds after its signal ends. What must be true of its phosphatase, and what is the cost of that design?
cards.back: The phosphatase must be fast, because the summed rates set how fast the level settles. Running it constantly costs ATP, so some pathways switch it on only when the signal ends.
cards.quote: a pathway that must shut off in seconds needs a fast phosphatase; running it constantly costs ATP
cards.section: How much protein carries the phosphate?

cards.front: About how many protein-kinase genes does the human genome hold, and about how many encode tyrosine kinases?
cards.back: About 518 kinase genes; about 90 encode tyrosine kinases.
cards.quote: The human genome holds about 518 protein-kinase genes.
cards.section: How the enzymes find the right targets

cards.front: Humans have hundreds of serine/threonine kinases but only a few dozen genes for serine/threonine phosphatase catalytic subunits. How can dephosphorylation still be specific?
cards.back: Each catalytic subunit pairs with many regulatory subunits that choose its location and substrates. PP1 has three genes but well over a hundred partners.
cards.quote: PP1, a major catalytic subunit, is encoded by three genes yet pairs with well over a hundred regulatory subunits, which choose its location and substrates.
cards.section: How the enzymes find the right targets

cards.front: What do the enzyme counts suggest about how tyrosine and serine/threonine dephosphorylation get their specificity, and how strong is that claim?
cards.back: Tyrosine dephosphorylation is steered more by enzyme choice, serine/threonine more by partner subunits. It is an inference from counts, not proof.
cards.quote: The counts suggest that tyrosine dephosphorylation is steered more by enzyme choice, and serine/threonine dephosphorylation by company.
cards.section: How the enzymes find the right targets

cards.front: About one in ten human kinases, called {{c1::pseudokinases}}, has lost catalytic activity and works by binding other proteins.
cards.quote: About one in ten human kinases, called pseudokinases, has lost catalytic activity and instead works by binding other proteins.
cards.section: Pseudokinases and family counts

cards.front: The tally 107 tyrosine phosphatases against 90 tyrosine kinases overstates the classical erasers. Why?
cards.back: It counts the whole phosphatase family. Only about 38 are classical phosphotyrosine-specific enzymes, and relatives such as PTEN prefer non-protein substrates.
cards.quote: only about 38 are classical phosphotyrosine-specific enzymes, and relatives such as PTEN prefer substrates other than proteins.
cards.section: Pseudokinases and family counts

cards.front: Of the roughly 90 human tyrosine kinases, {{c1::58}} are receptors spanning the plasma membrane with the kinase inside.
cards.quote: Of the roughly 90 human tyrosine kinases, 58 are receptors spanning the plasma membrane with the kinase inside.
cards.section: Pseudokinases and family counts

cards.front: Which three separate claims about a protein's phosphorylation need different kinds of evidence?
cards.back: The protein carries phosphate; a particular residue carries it; changing that site changes function.
cards.quote: Three claims need different evidence: the protein carries phosphate, a particular residue carries it, and changing that site changes function.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: A stimulated sample shows an extra, slower band on an SDS gel. What control ties the band to phosphate, and what does it leave open?
cards.back: Treat half the sample with purified phosphatase, with and without a phosphatase inhibitor. If the slow band collapses and the inhibitor prevents it, the shift depends on phosphate. The residue and function remain open.
cards.quote: If the slow band collapses into the fast one and a phosphatase inhibitor prevents that, the shift depends on phosphate.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: How can radioactivity show that a protein carries phosphate in cells?
cards.back: Grow cells with radioactive phosphate (32P), pull the protein out with an antibody and check for label.
cards.quote: Confirm that the protein carries phosphate by growing cells with radioactive phosphate (32P), pulling the protein out with an antibody and checking for label.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: How does mutating a candidate serine to alanine help map a phosphorylation site?
cards.back: Alanine removes the hydroxyl, so it cannot take phosphate. The site is the one whose change removes the label or the gel shift.
cards.quote: Change candidate serine or threonine residues to alanine, or tyrosine to phenylalanine, removing the hydroxyl, and ask which change removes the label or shift.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: In mass spectrometry, each phosphate adds {{c1::80 Da}} to a peptide.
cards.quote: each phosphate adds 80 Da to a peptide, and peptide fragments usually locate the residue.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: A peptide from the upper of two gel bands is 320 Da heavier than the matching peptide from the lower band, and the upper band runs an apparent 4 kDa higher. How many phosphates does the peptide carry, and what explains the 4 kDa?
cards.back: 320 / 80 = 4 phosphates. They add only 0.32 kDa, so the 4 kDa is apparent migration, not mass.
cards.quote: Three phosphates add only 0.24 kDa; the 3 kDa is apparent migration, not mass, so it cannot be converted into a phosphate count.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: In a site-function test, what do alanine and aspartate substitutions for a phosphorylatable serine each represent?
cards.back: Alanine cannot be phosphorylated. Aspartate's negative charge roughly imitates a persistent phosphate.
cards.quote: Compare an alanine mutant, which cannot be phosphorylated, with an aspartate mutant, whose negative charge roughly imitates a persistent phosphate.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: Enzyme E is active when kinase K is active. A threonine-20-to-aspartate mutant is active with or without kinase; a threonine-20-to-alanine mutant is inactive with or without kinase. What does this indicate?
cards.back: A phosphate on threonine 20 most likely turns the enzyme on. Alanine cannot be phosphorylated; aspartate roughly imitates a persistent phosphate.
cards.quote: Ask which of the four consequences the mimic reproduces: activity, docking, location or priming.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: A kinase phosphorylates a target serine at relative rates of 2, 100 and 35 when the residue four positions after it is alanine, phosphoserine or aspartate. What do the data say about priming and about aspartate as a mimic?
cards.back: A negative charge four positions away promotes phosphorylation, as in priming by an earlier phosphate. Aspartate gives about a third of the phosphoserine rate (35 vs 100). Rests on: phosphate carries about two charges, aspartate one.
cards.quote: Glycogen synthase kinase 3, for example, prefers a serine or threonine four residues before a site another kinase has phosphorylated.
cards.section: Four consequences of one added phosphate

cards.front: A kinase activates enzyme E. The serine-to-alanine mutant no longer responds to the kinase, but the serine-to-aspartate mutant is no more active than the unstimulated normal enzyme. What can you conclude?
cards.back: The alanine result points to this serine as the site that matters. The silent mimic proves little: aspartate carries one charge where phosphate carries two, so seek another line of evidence.
cards.quote: The alanine result points to this serine as the site that matters.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: A kinase is engineered to accept an ATP analog that normal kinases cannot use. What does labelling with the analog reveal?
cards.back: Only direct targets of that engineered kinase. This is how analog-sensitive kinases narrow the writer list.
cards.quote: Kevan Shokat's analog-sensitive kinases are engineered to accept an ATP analog that normal kinases cannot use, so they label only direct targets.
cards.section: Build the evidence: detect, map, test

cards.front: A radioactive spot ran between the phosphoserine and phosphothreonine markers and matched a phosphotyrosine standard. What did this reveal?
cards.back: That phosphotyrosine existed. Hunter and Sefton then showed that Src phosphorylates tyrosine.
cards.quote: Tony Hunter saw a radioactive spot between phosphoserine and phosphothreonine markers; his phosphotyrosine standard matched it.
cards.section: How reversible protein phosphorylation emerged

cards.front: A tumor cell loses a phosphatase that removes phosphate from a growth-promoting protein, with kinase activity unchanged. Predict the phosphorylated fraction and the effect on signaling.
cards.back: The fraction rises, because the brake is gone, so growth signaling persists. Rests on f = k(kinase)/(k(kinase) + k(phosphatase)).
cards.quote: Losing a phosphatase can cause similar damage because the brake is gone.
cards.section: When the switch breaks: kinases in disease and the clinic

cards.front: A small molecule is designed to fill the ATP pocket of one kinase. Why might it cause side effects?
cards.back: The ATP pocket is conserved, so the molecule may also fit some of the other 517 kinases. It must also compete with millimolar cellular ATP.
cards.quote: Conservation makes selectivity hard: a molecule fitting one ATP pocket may fit some of the other 517, causing side effects, and it must compete with millimolar cellular ATP.
cards.section: When the switch breaks: kinases in disease and the clinic

cards.front: Where do chemists find selectivity among kinase inhibitors, and how does imatinib illustrate it?
cards.back: At the pocket's edges, where kinases differ, or in inactive shapes only some kinases adopt. Imatinib binds Abl in an inactive conformation and spares most other kinases.
cards.quote: Imatinib binds Abl in an inactive conformation, helping explain why it spares most other kinases.
cards.section: When the switch breaks: kinases in disease and the clinic

cards.front: A compound inhibits purified kinase A half-maximally at 50 nM with 20 µM ATP, equal to the Km. With 2 mM ATP about 2.5 µM is needed, and at 2.5 µM it also inhibits two unrelated kinases. Explain both findings.
cards.back: The dose needed rose about 50-fold when ATP rose 100-fold, so the compound likely competes with ATP in the ATP pocket, which is conserved across kinases. Rests on: the ATP cleft is similar across kinases and drugs must compete with ATP.
cards.quote: The ATP cleft between the two lobes is snug and mostly greasy, so small drugs can fill it.
cards.section: When the switch breaks: kinases in disease and the clinic

cards.front: Transcription factor X is thought to be held in the cytoplasm by phosphates that calcineurin removes. Name one gel result and one mutant result that would support this.
cards.back: Gel: a slower band collapses with purified phosphatase and an inhibitor blocks that. Mutant: alanine at the candidate serine or threonine sites, which cannot be phosphorylated, would be expected to reach the nucleus without the signal. Rests on: the phosphatase control, alanine mutants and the NFAT case.
cards.quote: When calcineurin removes them, NFAT enters the nucleus: the eraser carries the signal.
cards.section: Four consequences of one added phosphate

cards.front: A regulatory subunit that targets PP1 to one substrate is depleted. Predict the effect on that substrate's phosphorylated fraction, and explain.
cards.back: Its fraction rises, because less phosphatase reaches it and k(phosphatase) falls in the denominator. Rests on: PP1 partners choose location and substrates, and f = k(kinase)/(k(kinase) + k(phosphatase)).
cards.quote: PP1, a major catalytic subunit, is encoded by three genes yet pairs with well over a hundred regulatory subunits, which choose its location and substrates.
cards.section: How the enzymes find the right targets
